passages.source_text: Ἀντίγραφον ἐπιστολῆς πρὸς Ἀππίωνα ὡς παρὰ τῆς ἐρωμένης. Θαυμάζω πῶς ἐπὶ σοφίᾳ με ἐπαινέσας ὡς ἀνοήτῳ γράφεις. εἰς γὰρ σὸν πάθος πεῖσαί με θελήσας ἐκ τῶν περὶ τοὺς θεοὺς μυθολογημάτων ἐποιήσω τὰ παραδείγματα, ἔρωτα τὸν πάντων πρεσβύτατον (ὡς ἔφης) ἐπὶ τῆς πάντων θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων, βλασφημῆσαι μὴ φοβηθείς, ὅπως τὴν ἐμὴν φθείρῃς ψυχὴν καὶ τὸ ἐμὸν σῶμα περιυβρίσῃς. ἔρως γὰρ θεῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀρχηγέτης ὁ ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις. εἰ γὰρ ἑκὼν ἐπιθυμεῖ, αὐτός ἐστιν ἑαυτοῦ πάθος καὶ κόλασις, καὶ θεὸς οὐκ ἂν εἴη ὁ πάσχων ἑκών· εἰ δὲ ἄκων ἐρᾷ τῆς μίξεως καὶ τὰς ἡμετέρας διερχόμενος ψυχὰς ὥσπερ δι’ ὀργάνων τῶν ἡμετέρων σωμάτων εἰς τὰς τῶν νοητῶν φέρεται συνουσίας, ὁ τοῦτον ἐρᾶν ποιῶν καὶ φέρων μείζων αὐτοῦ τυγχάνει· καὶ πάλιν αὐτοῦ ἐκείνου τοῦ φέροντος ἑτέρῳ πόθῳ φερομένου, μείζων ἄλλος ὁ φέρων ἐκεῖνον εὑρίσκεται καὶ εἰς ἀπέραντον ἐπαναφορὰ τῶν ἐρώντων γίνεται, ὅ ἐστιν ἀδύνατον. οὕτως οὐκ ἔστιν οὔτε ὁ φέρων οὔτε ὁ φερόμενος, ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἐρῶντος τὸ ἐπιθυμητικόν ἐστιν πάθος, ἐλπίδι αὐξόμενον καὶ ἀπογνώσει μειούμενον.

οἱ δὲ κρατεῖν αἰσχρᾶς ἐπιθυμίας μὴ βουλόμενοι τῶν θεῶν καταψεύδονται, ἵνα περὶ ὧν πράττουσιν τοὺς θεοὺς ὡς προτέρους δράσαντας ὑποδεικνύντες ἀπαλλάσσωνται τῆς μέμψεως. εἰ γὰρ παιδοποιίας ἕνεκεν καὶ οὐκ ἀσελγείας οἱ λεγόμενοι θεοὶ τὰς μοιχείας ἐπετέλουν, τί καὶ τοῖς ἄρσεσιν ἐμίγνυντο; ἀλλὰ χαριζόμενοι (φησίν) ταῖς ἐρωμέναις κατηστέριζον αὐτάς. οὐκοῦν πρὸ τούτου οὐκ ἦσαν ἀστέρες, μέχρις ὅτε ἀσελγείας προφάσει ὑπὸ μοιχῶν ὁ οὐρανὸς ἄστροις ἐκοσμήθη; πῶς δὲ καὶ οἱ τῶν κατηστερισμένων ἔκγονοι ἐν ᾅδου κολάζονται, ὅ τε Ἄτλας βαρούμενος καὶ ὁ Τάνταλος δίψῃ ἀνιώμενος καὶ ὁ Σίσυφος ἐρείδων πέτραν, Τιτυὸς τὰ σπλάγχνα διορυττόμενος, Ἰξίων περὶ τροχὸν ἀπαύστως κυλινδούμενος; πῶς δὲ καὶ οἱ ἐρασταί, θεοὶ ὄντες, οὓς ἐμίαναν κατηστέριζον, ἑαυτοῖς τοῦτο μὴ χαρισάμενοι;

οὐκ ἄρα ἦσαν θεοί, ἀλλὰ τυράννων αἰνίγματα. Κρόνου γὰρ ἐν τοῖς καυκασίοις ὄρεσιν (οὐκ ἐν οὐρανῷ ἀλλ’ ἐν γῇ) τάφος τις δείκνυται, ἀνδρὸς ἀγρίου καὶ τεκνοβόρου. ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦ ἀσελγοῦς Διός, τοῦ μυθικοῦ, τοῦ ὁμοίως τὴν θυγατέρα Μῆτιν καταπιόντος, ἐν Κρήτῃ θεωρεῖται τάφος. καὶ ἐν τῇ Ἀχερουσίᾳ δὲ λίμνῃ Πλούτωνος καὶ Ποσειδῶνος ἐν Τήνῳ, Ἡλίου δὲ ἐν Ἄτροις καὶ Σελήνης ἐν Κάρραις, Ἑρμοῦ δὲ ἐν Ἑρμουπόλει, Ἄρεως ἐν Θρᾴκῃ, Ἀφροδίτης ἐν Κύπρῳ, Διονύσου ἐν Θήβαις καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐν ἄλλοις τόποις. πλὴν φαίνονται αὐτῶν τῶν λεχθέντων θεῶν οἱ τάφοι· ἄνθρωποι γὰρ ἦσαν καὶ ταῦτα μοχθηροὶ καὶ μάγοι. οὐδὲ γὰρ ἄλλως μονοκράτορες ἐγεγόνεισαν (Ζεὺς λέγω ὁ μυθικὸς καὶ Διόνυσος), εἰ μὴ τῇ μεταμορφώσει ὧν ἤθελον ἐπεκράτουν εἰς ὅπερ αὐτοὶ ἤθελον.

εἰ δὲ τούτων δεῖ ζηλοῦν τοὺς βίους, μὴ μόνον τὰς μοιχείας, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς τραπέζας αὐτῶν μιμώμεθα. ὁ γὰρ Κρόνος τὰ αὐτοῦ τέκνα κατέπιεν καὶ Ζεὺς ὁμοίως τὴν αὐτοῦ θυγατέρα. καὶ τί δεῖ λέγειν; Πέλοψ πάντων θεῶν δεῖπνον ἐγένετο. ὅθεν καὶ ἡμεῖς πρὸ τῶν ἀθεμίτων γάμων ὅμοιον δεῖπνον τοῖς θεοῖς ἐπιτελέσωμεν. οὕτω γὰρ ἂν εἴη τὸ δεῖπνον τῶν γάμων ἄξιον. ἀλλὰ τοῦτο οὐκ ἂν ὑποσταίης ποτέ, ὡς οὐδὲ ἐγὼ τὸ μοιχήσασθαι. πρὸς τούτοις δέ μοι ἔρωτος ὡς δυνατοῦ θεοῦ ἀπειλεῖς χόλον. ἔρως θεὸς οὐκ ἔστιν οἷος δοκεῖ, ἀλλ’ ἐκ τῆς τοῦ ζῴου κράσεως πρὸς διαδοχὴν τοῦ βίου κατὰ πρόνοιαν τοῦ τὰ πάντα ἐνεργήσαντος συμβαίνουσα ἐπιθυμία, ἵνα τὸ πᾶν γένος μηδεπώποτε ἐπιλείπῃ, ἀλλὰ προφάσει ἡδονῆς ἐκ τῆς τοῦ μέλλοντος τελευτᾶν οὐσίας πάλιν ἄλλος γένηται, νομίμῳ προεκπεφυκὼς γάμῳ, ὅπως πρὸς τὸ γηροτροφεῖν τὸν αὐτοῦ πατέρα γνώσῃ· ὅπερ ποιεῖν οἱ ἐκ μοιχείας γεγονότες οὐκ ἂν ἐδύναντο, φύσιν στοργῆς πρὸς τοὺς γεννήσαντας οὐκ ἔχοντες.

ἐπεὶ οὖν διαδοχῆς ἕνεκεν καὶ γνησίας ἐπαυξήσεως (ὡς ἔφην) ἡ ἐπιθυμία συμβαίνει ἡ ἐρωτική, χρὴ τοὺς γονεῖς, σωφροσύνης προνοουμένους, τοὺς αὐτῶν παῖδας πρὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας διὰ τῶν σωφρονιζόντων βιβλίων προπαιδεύειν, καὶ τοῖς κρείττοσιν αὐτοὺς προεθίζειν λόγοις (ὅτι δευτέρα φύσις ἡ συνήθεια), πρὸς τούτοις δὲ πυκνῶς αὐτοὺς τὰς κολάσεις ὑπομιμνήσκειν τὰς ἐκ τῶν νόμων, ἵνα ὥσπερ χαλινῷ τῷ φόβῳ χρώμενοι ταῖς ἀτόποις μὴ συντρέχωσιν ἡδοναῖς. προσήκει δὲ καὶ πρὸ τοῦ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ἐπακμάσαι γάμῳ τὸ φυσικὸν τῆς ἡλικίας πληροφορεῖν πάθος, πρότερον πείσαντας εἰς εἶδος ἑταίρας γυναικὸς μὴ ἀτενίζειν.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text:
Copy of a letter to Appion, purportedly from the woman he loved.

I am amazed that, after praising me for wisdom, you write to me as though I were foolish. For in wishing to persuade me into your passion, you fashioned your examples from the mythic tales about the gods, with Love—the oldest of all, as you said—set over all gods and human beings, not fearing to blaspheme, so that you might corrupt my soul and outrage my body. For the love present in desires is not the leader of gods. If he desires willingly, he himself is his own passion and punishment, and one who suffers willingly could not be a god. But if he unwillingly loves sexual union and, passing through our souls as though by means of the organs of our bodies, is carried toward intercourse with those conceived in the mind, then the one who makes him love and drives him proves to be greater than he is. And again, when that very one who drives him is driven by another longing, another greater one is found who drives him, and there comes to be an endless regress of lovers, which is impossible. Thus there is neither one who drives nor one who is driven; rather, the desiring faculty of the lover himself is a passion, increased by hope and diminished by despair.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἀντίγραφον ἐπιστολῆς πρὸς Ἀππίωνα ὡς παρὰ τῆς ἐρωμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: Copy of a letter to Appion, purportedly from the woman he loved
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς παρὰ marks the represented or purported source of the letter; ἐρωμένη denotes the woman who is loved.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔρως γὰρ θεῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀρχηγέτης ὁ ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the love present in desires is not the leader of gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρχηγέτης can mean leader, originator, or founder; “leader” suits the ensuing argument about what might govern Love.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ δι’ ὀργάνων τῶν ἡμετέρων σωμάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: as though by means of the organs of our bodies
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὄργανα can denote instruments or bodily organs. “Instruments belonging to our bodies” remains a possible, more literal construal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὰς τῶν νοητῶν φέρεται συνουσίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: is carried toward intercourse with those conceived in the mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ νοητά literally denotes things or beings apprehended by thought. The contextual rendering treats them as the mentally conceived objects of desire; “unions with intelligible beings/things” is also grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ἀπέραντον ἐπαναφορὰ τῶν ἐρώντων γίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: there comes to be an endless regress of lovers
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπαναφορά here describes repeated referral from one moving cause to another, hence an infinite regress.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς πάντων θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων
source_issues.issue: The feminine article τῆς has no expressed feminine head noun. The translation construes the phrase elliptically as referring to Love’s position or dominion over all gods and human beings. Alternatively, the article may be a transmitted or printed intrusion.

passages.text: Those who are unwilling to master shameful desire tell lies about the gods, so that, by pointing to the gods as having done first the things they themselves do, they may escape blame. For if the so-called gods committed adultery for the sake of producing children and not from wantonness, why did they also have intercourse with males? “But,” he says, “as a favor to the women they loved, they placed them among the stars.” Then were there no stars before this, until heaven was adorned with stars by adulterers under the pretext of wantonness? And how is it that the descendants of those placed among the stars are punished in Hades—Atlas burdened with weight, Tantalus tormented by thirst, Sisyphus straining against a rock, Tityus having his entrails torn open, and Ixion ceaselessly rolled around a wheel? And how is it that the lovers, though they were gods, placed among the stars those whom they had defiled but did not grant this favor to themselves?

lexical_decisions.chosen: tell lies about the gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταψεύδομαι with the genitive means to speak falsely about or against someone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they placed them among the stars
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταστερίζω refers to catasterism, the mythical transformation or placement of a person among the stars.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Sisyphus straining against a rock
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐρείδω can mean press, push, brace, or strain against; the wording does not explicitly say that he rolls the rock.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Tityus having his entrails torn open
lexical_decisions.rationale: διορύσσω means dig or pierce through and here depicts the violent opening of his entrails.

passages.text: Therefore they were not gods but enigmas representing tyrants. For in the Caucasian Mountains—not in heaven but on earth—a tomb of Cronus is pointed out, the tomb of a savage, child-devouring man. A tomb of the wanton Zeus of myth, who similarly swallowed his daughter Metis, is also seen in Crete. There is also a tomb of Pluto at Lake Acherusia, one of Poseidon on Tenos, one of the Sun at Atroi and of the Moon at Carrhae, one of Hermes at Hermopolis, one of Ares in Thrace, one of Aphrodite on Cyprus, one of Dionysus at Thebes, and tombs of the others in other places. In short, the tombs of these so-called gods are visible, for they were human beings—wicked ones at that—and magicians. Indeed, they would not otherwise have become absolute rulers—I mean the mythical Zeus and Dionysus—if, by changing shape into whatever forms they themselves wished, they had not gained mastery over those they desired.

lexical_decisions.chosen: enigmas representing tyrants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive may describe enigmas about, belonging to, or representing tyrants; the context identifies the alleged gods as disguised accounts of human rulers.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a savage, child-devouring man
lexical_decisions.rationale: τεκνοβόρος denotes one who eats or devours children.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at Atroi
lexical_decisions.rationale: The place-name is transliterated directly because its precise historical identification is uncertain.

lexical_decisions.chosen: absolute rulers
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes persons exercising sole or exclusive power; “sole rulers” is an alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ μεταμορφώσει ὧν ἤθελον ἐπεκράτουν εἰς ὅπερ αὐτοὶ ἤθελον
lexical_decisions.chosen: by changing shape into whatever forms they themselves wished, they had ... gained mastery over those they desired
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering takes εἰς ὅπερ with μεταμορφώσει and understands the rulers themselves as changing shape. It is also syntactically possible to understand those over whom they gained mastery as being transformed into whatever the rulers wished.

passages.text: If, then, their lives must be emulated, let us imitate not only their adulteries but also their tables. For Cronus swallowed his own children, and Zeus likewise swallowed his own daughter. And what more needs to be said? Pelops became a dinner for all the gods. Therefore, before the forbidden marriages, let us also prepare a similar dinner for the gods. For in this way the dinner would be worthy of the marriages. But you would never submit to this, just as I would not submit to committing adultery. Besides this, you threaten me with the wrath of Love as a powerful god. Love is not a god of the kind he is thought to be, but a desire arising from the constitution of the living creature for the continuation of life, in accordance with the providence of the one who set all things in operation. Its purpose is that the entire race may never fail, but that, under the pretext of pleasure, another may come into being again from the substance of the one who is going to die, having sprung forth beforehand through lawful marriage, so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age. Those born from adultery would be unable to do this, because they have no natural affection for those who begot them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let us imitate ... their tables
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal image of their tables refers to their meals and dining practices, especially the cannibalistic meal mentioned next.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀλλὰ τοῦτο οὐκ ἂν ὑποσταίης ποτέ
lexical_decisions.chosen: you would never submit to this
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑφίστημι in this construction can mean undertake, endure, or submit to something.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from the constitution of the living creature
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρᾶσις literally concerns mixture or temperament and here denotes the creature’s natural constitution.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who set all things in operation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνεργέω emphasizes bringing things into activity or operation; “the one who produced all things” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having sprung forth beforehand through lawful marriage
lexical_decisions.rationale: προεκφύω depicts the child as coming forth before the parent’s death, while the dative γάμῳ identifies lawful marriage as the means.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως πρὸς τὸ γηροτροφεῖν τὸν αὐτοῦ πατέρα γνώσῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age
lexical_decisions.rationale: The placement permits “know his father for the purpose of supporting him.” The context contrasts identifiable lawful paternity with birth from adultery.

passages.text: Since, then, erotic desire arises for the sake of succession and legitimate increase, as I said, parents must, with a view to self-restraint, give their children preparatory education before desire arises, using books that teach self-control. They must also accustom them beforehand to the better teachings—for habit is a second nature—and, in addition, remind them frequently of the punishments prescribed by the laws, so that, using fear like a bridle, they may not rush into improper pleasures. It is also fitting, before desire reaches its full vigor, to satisfy through marriage the natural passion belonging to their age, having first persuaded them not to gaze intently upon the form of a courtesan.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for the sake of succession and legitimate increase
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνήσιος can mean genuine, legitimate, or lawfully born; the marital context favors “legitimate.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: using books that teach self-control
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφρονίζω means to make self-controlled, admonish, or train in sound conduct.

lexical_decisions.chosen: accustom them beforehand to the better teachings
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγοι can mean words, arguments, discourses, or teachings; the educational context favors “teachings.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: using fear like a bridle
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation retains the source’s image of fear restraining conduct as a bridle restrains an animal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γάμῳ τὸ φυσικὸν τῆς ἡλικίας πληροφορεῖν πάθος
lexical_decisions.chosen: to satisfy through marriage the natural passion belonging to their age
lexical_decisions.rationale: πληροφορέω can mean fill fully, fulfill, or satisfy; here its object is the natural passion of youth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς εἶδος ἑταίρας γυναικὸς μὴ ἀτενίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: not to gaze intently upon the form of a courtesan
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἑταίρα denotes a female companion or courtesan, while ἀτενίζω indicates fixed or intent looking.

"confirmed_print_features": [], "translation_policy_text": "# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
